narrative.summary: Monaco has no AI-specific law, strategy or public-sector AI guidance. AI is governed through its GDPR-style data protection law (Law No. 1.565 of 2024), which regulates decisions based solely on automated processing, requires information on their logic and impact assessments for profiling, and covers automated decisions by police and justice. The data protection authority (APDP) issued a critical opinion in December 2025 on a pending bill allowing police to use AI-based remote biometric identification. Monaco is a party to the Council of Europe's data protection convention (Convention 108).

narrative.review_notes: This review was carried out on 12 October 2026 from the official legal database (Legimonaco), the Journal de Monaco and the data protection authority's website. instruments.english_title: Law No. 1.565 of 3 December 2024 on the protection of personal data
instruments.issuing_authority: National Council (law sanctioned and promulgated by the Sovereign Prince)
instruments.current_status: Law dated 3 December 2024, published in the Journal de Monaco No. 8725 of 13 December 2024; it repeals Law No. 1.165 of 23 December 1993 (art. 118) and replaces the CCIN with the APDP (art. 107). Implemented by Sovereign Ordinance No. 11.327 of 10 July 2025. The text read contains no specific commencement clause, so effective_date is left null; art. 109 gives controllers one year from entry into force to bring existing processing into line.
instruments.summary: Monaco's GDPR-aligned general data protection law, replacing the 1993 law on nominative information and creating the Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP). Article 19 gives data subjects the right not to be subject to a decision with legal or similarly significant effects based solely on automated processing, including profiling (with contract, consent or legal-authorisation exceptions), articles 11-12 require information on the existence and logic of automated decision-making, and article 35 makes systematic profiling-based evaluation a high-risk case requiring a data protection impact assessment. For police and justice processing, article 67 prohibits solely automated adverse decisions unless authorised by ministerial order after the APDP's opinion with safeguards, and bans discriminatory profiling based on sensitive data.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding rules on automated decision-making, profiling and impact assessment that govern AI systems processing personal data in Monaco (Monaco is outside the EU, so the EU AI Act does not apply).

instruments.current_status: Opinion adopted 10 December 2025 on referral by the President of the National Council (8 October 2025) and published by the APDP. The bill it addresses (Government bill No. 1.087, tabled December 2023) was still pending before the National Council on 2026-10-12 (see leads). It follows CCIN deliberation No. 2023-066 of 26 April 2023 on the earlier draft, which was not made public.
instruments.summary: The APDP's opinion on Government bill No. 1.087, which would allow the police to use AI-based remote biometric (facial) identification on public video surveillance to find wanted or flagged persons. It compares the bill with the EU AI Act's restrictions on real-time remote biometric identification and finds the legal framework insufficient, citing the dual regime of Law No. 1.430 and Law No. 1.565, the absence of a mandatory impact assessment for police processing, and the risk of extension by regulation. It asks for safeguards including controls on training-data quality and ethics, disclosure of algorithmic bias and of acceptable false-positive and false-negative thresholds, display of the AI's confidence score, human verification, and clear liability for the AI provider.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Regulator's expectations for police use of AI facial recognition; the main AI-specific regulatory text published in Monaco.
